newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU could make UK commodity houses increase capital.
newsitem.headline: EU could make UK commodity houses increase capital.

text.p: The European Commission is expected to propose rules on Wednesday that could force British commodities trading houses to increase capital to cover market risks, industry and Commission officials said.
Although the proposal is not targeted at Britain, it would particularly affect the London commodities market, where some 95 percent of the EU's commodity business is conducted.

The plan is part of a broader proposal to incorporate in EU legislation a 1995 agreement by the Basle Committee on Banking Supervision which allows banks to use internal models to calculate the capital required to protect against market risks.
The problem arises because the Basle accord, which covers banks in the world's 10 richest nations, sets a single capital requirement for commodities based on the most volatile products such as oil.
Banks preferred this approach to a complex grading of the different commodities given that commodities trading is only a marginal part of their business.

But EU-based investment firms and particularly those which trade mainly in commodities, which had no say in the Basle talks, find themselves trapped as the Commission incorporates the Basle agreement into the 1993 Capital Adequacy Directive which applies to both banks and investment firms.
The solution, Commission officials say, would be for commodities trading firms to also use internal risk management models to recognise the different price volatilities of each product traded.
But the risk involved in trading commodities, especially commodities derivatives such as options, is difficult to measure and the models are simply not available off the peg, one official said.

The British government has expressed its opposition to extending the rules to commodities trading, but it seems likely to win only a grace period whose duration would be decided on Wednesday by the Commission, industry and Commission sources said.
"A transition period to deal with commodities is under discussion," one Commission source said.
"We have done the maximum to accomodate the British views, to give them the time necessary to adapt to the new rules," another EU official said.

European banks unanimously welcome the adoption of the Basle accord, saying that it will translate into a reduction of their capital requirements because of a more accurate measurement of market risk.
The proposal on the modification of the 1993 directive on capital adequacy of investment firms and credit institutions will have to be approved by a qualified majority of EU members.
European banks are eager to see the new set of capital charges come into force to avoid being put at disadvantage with their non-EU rivals. The Basle accord becomes effective at the end of this year.

"Authorising the use of internal models is very important because they are believed to be much more sophisticated than the existing standardised models and this would reduce the capital requirements of banks", Breda Lynch, an adviser at the European Banking Federation, told Reuters.
